planting.note: Set container-grown plants in fall or spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered spot with partial shade; this is among the earliest-blooming bholua selections, originating from seed collected in Darjeeling and raised at RHS Garden Wisley.

directions: Choose a sheltered spot with east, west, or north aspect protected from harsh midday sun and drying winds, since bholua selections dislike baking heat and exposure. Darjeeling is a semi-evergreen, upright form with tan stems and glossy mid-green leaves that opens clusters of pale pink, intensely fragrant flowers from early winter, among the earliest of the bholua clones to open, fading to near-white as they age. Keep soil consistently moist but free-draining and avoid disturbing the roots once sited, since daphnes resent transplanting; light staking may help the upright growth in windy gardens. All plant parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in fall or spring in sheltered, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this selection was made at Kew's Wakehurst Place from seed collected on Nepal's Daman Ridge by Sir Peter Smithers and carries an RHS Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Site in a wind-sheltered border in partial shade where the tall, slender habit won't be battered by storms; light staking helps keep the upright stems vertical as the shrub matures. Deep purplish-pink buds open from midwinter into early spring to paler pink, heavily scented flowers that darken again with age, followed by black berries. Grow in moist but free-draining, low-nutrient soil and avoid root disturbance after planting, since this and other bholua cultivars establish slowly and dislike being moved. All plant parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in sheltered, moist but well-drained soil in partial shade; this hybrid between D. bholua 'Jacqueline Postill' and the hardier D. acutiloba 'Fragrant Cloud' was raised by British nurseryman Robin White for improved cold tolerance and a bushier habit than straight bholua selections.

directions: Grow in a sheltered partial-shade position with consistently moist, humus-rich, free-draining soil, the same conditions favored by its D. bholua parent. Spring Herald forms a bushier, more compact evergreen shrub than typical bholua cultivars and extends the bloom season, opening cream-tinged, clove-scented flowers over a long period from midwinter into late spring rather than in one concentrated flush. Because it carries genes from the hardier D. acutiloba parent, it tolerates colder sites better than most bholua selections, though it still resents root disturbance once established. All plant parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in fall or spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial sun to partial shade; this New Zealand-bred hybrid of D. odora 'Grace Stewart' and D. bholua, raised by Mark Jury, was selected for larger flowers and better heat and sun tolerance than typical winter daphnes.

directions: Site in partial sun to partial shade, giving afternoon shade in hot-summer climates even though this hybrid tolerates more direct sun than most daphnes. Bred in New Zealand by crossing D. odora 'Grace Stewart' with D. bholua, it produces blooms noticeably larger than typical D. odora flowers in dense, fragrant pink clusters from midwinter into spring. Plant in evenly moist, sharply drained soil and avoid wet feet or heavy fertilizing, since excess richness can push soft growth that is more prone to dieback. All plant parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in dry to average, very well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Maejima carries a noticeably wider cream-to-yellow leaf margin than the related 'Aureomarginata', of which it is a sport, making it the most heavily variegated of the common winter daphne selections.

directions: Grow in dry to average moisture and sharply drained soil in full sun to partial shade; a slow grower, it rewards patience over a long lifespan rather than quick coverage. From late winter into early spring it opens richly fragrant dark pink flower clusters that read as a sharp contrast against the glossy green leaves edged in broad cream to yellow margins, a wider band of variegation than most other D. odora selections show. Keep roots undisturbed after planting and avoid soggy sites, which quickly cause crown rot in this species. All plant parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist but well-drained, acid to neutral soil in full to partial shade; as a male clone, Finchy produces no berries itself but supplies pollen to nearby female skimmias such as 'Kew Green' or 'Rubella'.

directions: Grow in moist, humus-rich, acid to neutral soil in full or partial shade with a sheltered aspect, tolerating some morning or afternoon sun if the soil stays damp. Finchy is a compact, dense male selection with glossy dark green leaves that bears crowded panicles of small, fragrant, star-shaped creamy-white flowers in spring, making it a reliable pollen source rather than a berrying plant. Pair it with a female Skimmia japonica cultivar within pollinating distance to ensure the female sets its showy red fruit. Avoid chalky or waterlogged soils, both of which quickly cause chlorosis or root problems in this species.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial sun to full shade; this clump-forming, non-suckering selection from the legendary Western Hills Nursery in California is the first known red-fruited form of Sarcococca x confusa.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial sun to deep shade, where upright stems clothed in small, narrow, glossy green leaves form a tidy, non-suckering clump reminiscent of poet's laurel. Tiny, intensely fragrant white flowers open along the stems in late winter, followed starting in early January by bright red fruit, a distinctive break from the black fruit typical of most sweet box selections. It tolerates dry woodland soils once established but is intolerant of soggy sites, so avoid low spots that collect winter moisture.
